title: Producer prices and Nvidia's leadership void set Friday's tone
dek: US stock futures are little changed and mixed ahead of the 8:30 a.m. producer price report, after a week in which hot consumer inflation pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back above 5% and Nvidia lost its founding CEO. Nvidia is edging higher before the bell, while chip rivals that rallied Thursday give back some gains.
quick: October PPI is due at 8:30 a.m. ET; forecasters expect a 0.4% monthly rise, cooler than September's 1.3%.
The 10-year Treasury yield closed near 5.12% Thursday, its biggest multi-day jump since 2022, as traders price a December Fed rate hike.
Nvidia rose about 1% to 2% pre-market after a roughly 4% drop Thursday on Jensen Huang's resignation; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
Five Fed officials speak today, starting with Boston's Susan Collins at 9:10 a.m. ET.
The yen touched 160 per dollar, a level where Tokyo intervened over the summer; Japanese officials are again warning against fast moves.
Bitcoin slipped below $70,000 for the first time since August amid continued ETF outflows.

blocks.head: Producer prices are the last big inflation test before the Fed meets
blocks.what: The Labor Department releases October producer prices at 8:30 a.m. ET. Forecasts compiled for the economic calendar call for a 0.4% monthly rise in headline PPI and 0.3% in core, after September jumps of 1.3% and 0.7%. On Tuesday, consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices 0.3%, both a tenth above forecasts. The BLS could not publish annual rates because it did not collect October 2025 data during last year's government shutdown.
blocks.why: Another hot reading would back up rate-hike bets and could push Treasury yields and the dollar higher, a headwind for rate-sensitive stocks such as small caps, homebuilders and high-valuation tech. A cooler print could ease some of the pressure that sent bond yields up sharply this week.
blocks.watch: Components that feed into the Fed's preferred PCE gauge, such as airfares, portfolio management fees and medical services.

blocks.head: A December rate hike is now close to fully priced
blocks.what: After the CPI report, CME FedWatch showed about an 88% chance of a quarter-point increase at the December 9 meeting, up from about 72% a week earlier. Some trading on Tuesday also priced roughly a 1-in-7 chance of a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said a larger hike should be considered if core inflation came in around 0.3%, the figure the BLS then reported, though he said he could still support a quarter-point move. The Fed raised its target range to 3.75% to 4% in September and held in October.
blocks.why: Higher expected policy rates lift short-term yields and the dollar and raise borrowing costs for companies and households. Strategists quoted by CNBC called the Fed the main medium-term risk for stocks if it tightens more than markets expect.
blocks.watch: Today's Fed speakers for any comments on the size of a December move.

blocks.head: Nvidia begins life without Jensen Huang
blocks.what: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with an employee and one with a woman U.S. officials suspect of spying for China, according to the WSJ, NYT and CNBC. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey Jones was named board chair. Nvidia shares closed down about 4% on Thursday and rose roughly 1% to 2% pre-market, per Investing.com and other outlets. Huang has agreed to testify before the House, BBC and TechCrunch reported.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, so its moves drive index-fund returns. Thursday's trading split the AI group: AMD and Broadcom each rose more than 5% on bets they could gain share, while companies that depend on Nvidia for chips or financing came under pressure.
blocks.watch: Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, its first report under interim leadership.

blocks.head: Huang affair raises the stakes for China chip policy and the Trump-Xi summit
blocks.what: The scandal has renewed calls in Congress to tighten exports of advanced AI chips to China. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked the administration to preserve records about Nvidia's China chip exports, and Sen. Tom Cotton urged Commerce to blacklist Chinese memory maker CXMT, CNBC and the WSJ reported. President Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.
blocks.why: Tighter export rules would weigh on chipmakers with China sales, including Nvidia, AMD and equipment makers, and could raise trade tensions ahead of the summit. Hong Kong and Chinese tech shares fell overnight.

blocks.head: Oil rebounds as Trump says the US does not need an Iran deal
blocks.what: Brent crude settled about 3.3% higher on Thursday near $95.80 a barrel, and WTI rose about 2.6% to around $88.70, after President Trump posted that Washington does not need a deal with Iran, according to CNBC and Bloomberg via Rigzone. Reuters reported the US blockade on Iranian oil shipments and sanctions would stay in place. Houthi claims of attacks on Saudi energy facilities also added to supply worries.
blocks.why: Higher oil feeds directly into inflation expectations and bond yields, which matters more than usual with a Fed hike on the table. Energy was the only S&P 500 sector to gain on Thursday.
blocks.watch: Oil had fallen sharply last week; Reuters noted Brent is still on track for a weekly loss.

blocks.head: Earnings: Cisco, Applied Materials and Cerebras report AI-driven growth
blocks.what: Cisco beat estimates with adjusted earnings of $1.40 a share on $18.52 billion in revenue and raised its target for AI infrastructure revenue from large cloud customers to $9 billion for the fiscal year, from $7.5 billion. Applied Materials reported revenue of about $10.4 billion, up 53% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings above forecasts. Cerebras jumped about 17% after hours on stronger revenue and a new Microsoft deal, CNBC reported.
blocks.why: The reports point to continued AI spending even as Nvidia's leadership turmoil raises questions about the sector, which could steady chip and network-equipment stocks.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets were mixed and mostly lower. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed up about 0.5% near 61,140, helped by chip stocks after a sharp selloff earlier in the week. South Korea's Kospi fell about 1%, Shanghai's Composite slipped about 0.5%, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost more than 1%, with Chinese tech under pressure from the Nvidia fallout and talk of tighter chip rules. SoftBank, a major OpenAI investor, fell about 5%, the AP reported.
Europe

European stocks opened slightly lower. The Stoxx 600 fell about 0.2%, London's FTSE 100 lost about 0.2%, and the CAC 40 and DAX were each down about 0.3% early, according to the AP and Euronews. Chip-equipment makers led the decline, with ASML and ASM International down about 1.5%. On Thursday, the UK reported third-quarter growth of 0.7%, in line with estimates.
Currencies

The dollar index is little changed near 103.2. The yen is the main story: the dollar touched about 160 yen on Thursday and again early Friday, the first time above that level since September. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned against one-sided moves, and top currency official Atsushi Mimura said the yen had moved too fast. Japan and the US jointly intervened in late July and early August, when Tokyo spent a record 15.4 trillion yen. The euro trades near $1.106, the pound near $1.322, and the dollar near 6.67 yuan, all within a narrow range.

Why it matters: a stronger dollar on rate-hike bets is pushing on the yen, and any intervention by Tokyo could cause sharp moves in the yen and spill over into Japanese stocks and global bond markets.

US stock futures are mixed and close to flat before the PPI report. S&P 500 and Dow futures are up slightly, while Nasdaq 100 futures are a bit weaker as AMD and Broadcom give back part of Thursday's gains and Nvidia rebounds modestly. Thursday's session ended with the S&P 500 down 0.35% at 7,592, the Dow down 0.36% and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.39%, after the S&P recovered from a sharper early drop.

Small caps were hit hardest Thursday: the Russell 2000 fell about 1.7%, consistent with rising yields hurting smaller, more debt-reliant companies. The VIX volatility index rose about 7% to 18.7, elevated but below panic levels. The 8:30 a.m. data will likely set the direction for the open.

Treasury yields jumped this week as bond markets reopened after Veterans Day. On Thursday the 2-year yield rose about 15 basis points to around 4.86%, the 10-year rose about 13 basis points to roughly 5.12%, back above 5%, and the 30-year rose about 10 basis points to near 5.45%, CNBC reported. MarketWatch said the 2-year's four-session rise was the largest since June 2022. Yields are little changed this morning.

The curve remains upward sloping: the 10-year sits about 26 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year about 59 basis points above. With the Fed's range at 3.75% to 4%, the 2-year yield well above the funds rate shows traders expect more hikes. Fed funds futures, as tracked by CME FedWatch, show a December quarter-point hike as highly likely, with a smaller chance of a half point.

Waller's openness to a larger move after the CPI report was the most notable signal from officials this week. Separately, the Fed said it will hold seven policy votes in 2027 and use its October 2027 meeting for discussion only, with no rate vote or statement, CNBC reported.
Fed speakers today (ET)

items: 9:10 a.m.: Boston Fed President Susan Collins
9:40 a.m.: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan

blocks.text: Thursday's sectors

Energy was the only S&P 500 sector to rise Thursday, up about 1.5%, as oil rebounded. Materials led the declines, down about 1.3%, as gold and other metals fell while rising yields and a firmer dollar weighed. Communication services and industrials each fell about 0.9%, and financials lost about 0.7%. Technology fell a more modest 0.3% because gains in AMD and Broadcom offset most of Nvidia's drop. Utilities were roughly flat, holding up better than other rate-sensitive groups.
Pre-market movers

items: Nvidia: up roughly 1% to 2% after Thursday's roughly 4% drop on the CEO change; analysts have been revisiting ratings.
AMD and Broadcom: each down roughly 2% to 3% after gaining more than 5% Thursday.
Cerebras: up about 16% to 18% on stronger-than-expected revenue and a Microsoft deal; outlets noted a wider loss and some contract delays.
Cisco: mixed in early trading after beating forecasts and raising its AI revenue target.
Applied Materials: roughly flat after revenue grew 53% and results came in above forecasts.
Nebius: fell about 16% Thursday after raising its spending plans and giving a weak outlook; AI cloud providers remain sensitive to financing questions.

blocks.text: Oil

Oil is easing slightly this morning after Thursday's jump, with WTI near $88 and Brent near $95.50. Thursday's rally followed the president's Iran comments and Houthi attack claims, partly offset by a 4.7 million barrel rise in US crude stockpiles reported by the EIA. Brent is still headed for a weekly loss after a 16% drop last week, Reuters reported.
Gold

Gold is up about 1% near $3,920 an ounce after hitting a 13-month low near $3,850 on Thursday as yields rose, Kitco and other outlets reported. It remains well below its 2026 record. Higher real yields and a firm dollar have weighed on gold, since it pays no interest.
Crypto

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time since August and traded near $68,000 early Friday, down about 4% over 24 hours. Ether fell about 5% to around $1,915. US spot bitcoin ETFs have seen about $1.5 billion of withdrawals since November 5, according to Farside Investors data. Pressure has continued since Binance's roughly $6.4 billion hack in late October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea-linked hackers, along with rising rate expectations and leveraged-position liquidations.

items: 8:30 a.m. ET, October PPI: the main release. Consensus is 0.4% for the headline and 0.3% for core, down from 1.3% and 0.7% in September. A reading at or above forecast would support December hike pricing.
Fed speakers throughout the day (see Rates & the Fed): listen for views on a quarter-point versus a half-point hike.
10:15 a.m. ET, quarterly mortgage delinquency data: last at 4.37%; a check on household strain as mortgage rates rise.
10:30 a.m. ET, EIA natural gas storage: delayed a day by the holiday; forecast is a 65 billion cubic foot build, versus 77 billion last week.

blocks.text: Friday's earnings calendar is light. The largest companies on it are Japanese banks reporting in Tokyo hours. The big tech reports came after Thursday's close and are covered above.

rows: Lending margins as the Bank of Japan weighs a rate hike; consensus about $0.24 per ADR share
Net interest income and any change to full-year profit targets; consensus about $0.21 per ADR share
Production volumes and lithium pricing as a read on EV battery demand
Revenue growth and path to profitability; consensus loss of $0.07 a share
Bitcoin-holding company; results tied to bitcoin's slide this month

blocks.text: Today ends the week, and next week is busy. Nvidia reports on Tuesday, November 17, its first quarter under interim CEO Colette Kress. Analysts polled by LSEG expect revenue of about $108.9 billion, up about 91% from a year earlier, and investors will be listening for any change in demand or in China-related guidance. President Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, with trade, Taiwan and chip exports likely on the agenda. Anthropic's initial public offering is scheduled for November 19, according to Reuters. Minutes of the Fed's October meeting and more retail earnings, including Walmart, are also expected. All of this comes with the 10-year yield above 5% and a December Fed hike largely priced in, so data and company guidance could move yields and stocks more than usual.

bottom_line: The setup is cautious but steady: futures are flat, bond yields are holding this week's sharp gains, and Nvidia is stabilizing after its CEO's exit. The 8:30 a.m. producer price report and five Fed speakers will likely set the direction for rates and stocks heading into next week's Nvidia earnings and the Trump-Xi summit.
